item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How Israel has engineered a system of apartheid on West Bank roads
item.description:
How Israel has engineered a system of apartheid on West Bank roads

Submitted by Fareed Taamallah on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 21:13
Every afternoon, Palestinian commuters sit behind military gates while Israeli settlers drive on. The system is built to exhaust them and make staying on their land harder
Israeli forces close a military checkpoint near the Palestinian town of Taybeh, east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, on 23 August 2026, after shooting and wounding a Palestinian man from the nearby village of Burqa (Zain Jaafar/AFP)
Off

Every afternoon at exactly 4pm, a calculated military decision transforms the exits of Ramallah and al-Bireh into an open-air gridlock of vehicles piled nose to tail, idling engines and mounting frustration.

What Israeli authorities continue to market to the world as temporary "security measures" - the iron gates, concrete barriers, earth mounds and armed checkpoints choking the occupied West Bank - has long since metastasised into a deliberate, institutionalised apparatus of spatial segregation and racial discrimination.

This architecture of control does not exist to neutralise genuine threats. It operates to clear shared arterial roads for Israeli settlers at the exact hour Palestinian civilian movement reaches its daily peak.

By subordinating the basic right of an indigenous population to travel through its own land, the system grants permanent priority to one group while punishing another for the simple act of trying to commute home after a day's work.

According to comprehensive field documentation compiled by the United Nations' humanitarian office, Ocha, and the human rights organisation B'Tselem, the landscape of the occupied West Bank is carved up by more than 900 fixed and intermittent movement obstacles.

They comprise permanently manned military checkpoints, partial ones, remote-controlled iron gates, earth mounds, roadblocks and trenches, which restrict and dictate the daily lives of 3.4 million Palestinians.

Ocha counts 232 iron gates alone, at least 120 installed in 2025, and the Palestinian commission that monitors the wall and settlements now puts the total at 942.

Within the immediate vicinity of Ramallah and al-Bireh alone, some 160 of these closure points exist, a count exceeded only in Hebron, acting as constant choke points along the transit corridors that connect the governorate to the north, east and south of the West Bank.

To the south, Palestinian vehicular movement is funnelled through Qalandia, Jaba and the northern Jerusalem access routes, where dense local traffic intersects with bypass highways engineered to connect Israeli settlements to population centres inside the separation wall.

What was originally justified under the flimsy pretext of defence has evolved into a calculated instrument of systemic discrimination and population management

To the north, the critical arteries pass through the Ein Siniya and Atara checkpoints, the Yabrud junction and the Beit El checkpoint, known locally as the DCO after the Israeli military's District Coordination Office beside it.

The Israeli separation wall, 85 percent of which runs inside the West Bank, and its interlocking network of checkpoints have long ceased to function as anything like a border. Operating deep inside occupied territory, they actively reshape geography to annex settlement blocs, isolate Palestinian communities in fragmented enclaves and re-engineer public space.

By dictating who may travel, when, and along which permitted bypasses, the system establishes a permanent hierarchy of spatial privilege. What was originally justified under the flimsy pretext of defence has evolved into a calculated instrument of systemic discrimination and population management.

Punishing the victims

The mechanics of this structural discrimination are felt with devastating consistency each afternoon on every side of the Beit El (DCO) checkpoint. Before October 2023, this strategic crossing operated on a 24-hour basis, a fact documented by field monitors.

The army closed it outright after 7 October 2023 and reopened it to Palestinian traffic in June 2024, as Israeli settlers stoned cars at the gate and demanded that it remain closed to us. The head of the Beit El settlement council called the reopening "folly".

Crossings that were once open around the clock now close during the morning and evening rush hours. At the DCO, under arbitrary military mandates, the checkpoint is abruptly closed to Palestinian vehicular traffic in both directions at 4pm sharp, remaining shut until 9pm to clear the roadway for settlers.

This timing is neither random nor dictated by the physical capacity of the road. It coincides precisely with the period when thousands of workers, students and residents attempt to exit Ramallah and al-Bireh to return to their surrounding towns and villages. Simultaneously, this window sees increased traffic from Israeli settlers travelling along the same regional arteries.

As olive harvest nears, Palestinian farmers urgently need international protection
Read More »

Rather than addressing the primary source of tension on these corridors, where armed Israeli settlers have frequently intercepted, stoned and attacked Palestinian vehicles under cover of night, the occupation authorities consistently resort to collective punishment.

By shutting down the checkpoint to Palestinian drivers at 4pm, the military clears the thoroughfare, allowing settlers to travel with total freedom and speed, unencumbered by the presence of Palestinian commuters who might otherwise share the road and create perceived congestion.

The security narrative collapses under field analysis. When a vital transit artery is arbitrarily closed, the vehicular flow does not dissipate; it is forcibly redirected onto narrow secondary roads. This creates cascading bottlenecks across adjacent checkpoints, compounding the regional crisis and leaving an entire population's daily existence tethered to unpredictable military decrees.

The same decrees now operate on a larger scale. For a week from 25 September, over the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, Israel sealed the West Bank; the Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints and the gates of Nabi Saleh and Taybeh were closed; and at Jaba, commuters spent the night in their cars.

On 27 October, every entrance to Ramallah was shut, and new checkpoints were set up on the alternative roads residents use to get around them.

The micro-physics of humiliation

The systematic suppression of Palestinian movement is executed not only through outright road closures, but through the deliberate, micro-calculated elongation of transit times at active checkpoints. Passing through a military checkpoint is rarely a straightforward verification process; it has been crafted into a tedious, multi-stage ritual designed to exhaust, delay and demoralise.

A driver approaches the stop line, comes to a complete halt and is instructed to switch off the engine. They must exit the vehicle in all weather conditions, walk towards an armed soldier positioned behind armoured glass or concrete blocks, and present their identification card and vehicle registration.

Once these are handed back, the driver is instructed to return to the vehicle, only to be ordered onto a secondary inspection zone. There, their details may undergo computer verification, photographic logging or extended background checks. Only after this repetitive sequence is completed can they restart the vehicle and drive off.

Even under ideal conditions, a single inspection lane bogged down by these contrived bureaucratic hurdles can process no more than 12 to 15 vehicles an hour. When thousands of cars are forced into single-file inspection channels, administrative friction multiplies into mile-long queues and hours of wasted time.

Beyond the immense economic toll of lost labour hours and fuel, these checkpoints frequently become sites of casual cruelty and entertainment for bored, emboldened soldiers. The systematic normalisation of petty humiliation converts basic daily travel into an exercise in psychological attrition, designed to reinforce a status of total subjugation.

This macro-structure of fragmentation and control is not merely an analytical concept; it is a deeply personal, lived reality. During my regular trips between Ramallah, where I live, and my birthplace, the village of Qira in Salfit governorate, the physical and emotional weight of these checkpoints becomes strikingly personal.

What should be a straightforward 40-minute drive through my home landscape has become an unpredictable gauntlet of military barriers, iron gates and sudden shutdowns. Each journey requires navigating a landscape of constant uncertainty, where minor procedural delays or arbitrary gate closures can turn a routine commute into an hours-long ordeal.

This manufactured hardship is shared by hundreds of thousands of Palestinians across the West Bank, serving as a constant daily reminder of an institutional directive aimed at making everyday life as exhausting and precarious as possible.

'De facto sovereignty'

In February 2023, weeks after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned to office at the head of a far-right coalition, his government handed Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and himself a settler, civilian authority over the occupied West Bank, including settlement planning and the Civil Administration that rules Palestinian life.

The gates multiplied. Since October 2023, B'Tselem has counted more than 200 new checkpoints, and the Association for Civil Rights in Israel has told the High Court that some of the roadblocks were first erected by settlers, with the army taking them over afterwards.

Meanwhile, the roads are being rebuilt for the settlers. In July 2025, Smotrich announced 918 million shekels ($275m) for West Bank roads, including bypasses so that Israeli motorists can avoid Palestinian towns. "This is how you do de facto sovereignty," he said. In May 2026, the government added $270m for roads linking 20 settlements and outposts.

The settlers who use those roads have never been more violent. The 397 settler attacks Ocha logged in October were the most it has recorded in any month since it began counting in 2006.

In defence of Israel's Jewish settlers in the West Bank
Read More »

Human Rights Watch counts 107 Palestinian communities fully or partly displaced since January 2023. B'Tselem, in its September report on the West Bank, calls a closed gate "an instrument" of dispossession and elimination.

International legal frameworks and human rights documentation unequivocally classify these measures not as legitimate defensive precautions but as severe violations of the fundamental right to freedom of movement. The International Court of Justice found the wall contrary to international law in 2004 and Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful in 2024.

What is marketed under the sanitised label of "security policy" is nothing less than an institutionalised system of apartheid, as Amnesty International and B'Tselem have both documented. It is the direct expression of an Israeli Zionist racist mentality that views Palestinians not as human beings with equal rights to their own land, but as an inconvenience to be cleared away.

While this apparatus of control generates immense daily suffering and fuels a justified, burning anger, it ultimately fails in its primary ambition. The occupation may choke our roads, steal our hours and turn simple commutes into gruelling daily battles, but it will never erase our presence or break our resolve.

We will suffer, we will rage, but we will not leave. Every Palestinian who waits through the bottlenecks returns home to their village and remains rooted on their ancestral land, turning the simple act of staying into an unyielding refutation of quiet displacement.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Palestinian families brace for expulsion as settlers erect outpost near West Bank village
item.description:
Palestinian families brace for expulsion as settlers erect outpost near West Bank village

Submitted by Tamara Davison on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 13:13
For people in Jiftlik, in the Jordan Valley, the arrival of Israeli settlers brings renewed threats of violence, land seizures and forced displacement
Residents of al-Shuneh cluster in West Bank's Jordan Valley keep watch after settlers set up an outpost in the nearby hilltop (Tamara Davison/MEE)
Off

Mohammed* sips coffee outside his small concrete home in the al-Shuneh cluster, framed by the sprawling Jordan Valley in the occupied West Bank. 

But the energy abruptly shifts when a pickup truck kicks up dust and hurtles down the hillside: it’s Israeli settlers. 

He quickly ushers his guests toward the door, watching anxiously until the car passes into the distance. 

“The attacks are escalating,” the Palestinian man says, his young children cautiously peering out of the doorway of his family home. 

“There's this feeling of insecurity, living in this constant limbo.” 

Around 80 Palestinian families rely on the remote rocky hillside on the eastern slopes of the West Bank, overlooking the Jordan River.

Al-Shuneh is one of the four population clusters in the agricultural village of Jiftlik, north of the city of Jericho.

The village's population consists of farmers and nomads who rely on livestock raising for their livelihoods.

'He told me... I should go to Europe, Canada, or places like that'

- Mohammed, al-Shuneh resident  

Many were born in al-Shuneh to families displaced by Israeli forces decades ago from other parts of Palestine.

But their livelihoods have been upended by a slow and ongoing torment: lingering Israeli demolition orders and, more recently, the subsequent arrival of hostile settlers. 

As Israel headed to the polls on 27 October for parliamentary elections, al-Shuneh was disrupted by the sight of new tents and Israeli flags mounted on the hilltop just two minutes away from Mohammed’s home, adding to an already growing atmosphere of intimidation.

The armed group installed water and electricity cables and released a video featuring drone footage, settler interviews, and clips of a mother with a young baby on social media, encouraging others to join them. 

It’s one of the latest Israeli outposts established in the Jordan Valley, which are illegal under both Israeli domestic law and international law. 

According to the townspeople, the message delivered in the run-up to the outpost’s establishment was clear: “If [Benjamin] Netanyahu wins, leave on your own. If [Gadi] Eisenkot wins, we will make sure you are displaced.” 

While votes were still being counted in Israel on 28 October, masked settlers encircled several homes in the early hours of the morning, threatening the families. 

Israeli forces demolish five West Bank buildings and displace over 100 Palestinians
Read More »

“You don't know what the future holds, or where you'll be tomorrow,” Mohammed tells Middle East Eye. “Your hands are shackled.”

The Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission said Israeli settlers attempted to establish 28 new outposts and committed 1,369 attacks in October alone across the West Bank. 

It’s a sign that Israeli settler strategies are escalating rapidly despite political shifts.

At this outpost, settler numbers are thought to have risen to almost 20 in the days after its establishment, and aggressive rhetoric is growing. 

When Mohammed asked one of the settlers walking on his land where else he was supposed to go, he was told anywhere but his homeland. 

“He told me that there’s no future for my children here or me, and that I should go to Europe, Canada, or places like that.”

Fears of forced displacement

The road towards al-Shuneh on the outskirts of Jiftlik meanders through rolling hills, past date forests and settlements emblazoned with Israeli flags. Along the way, the empty shells of destroyed buildings that once housed other thriving Palestinian villages increasingly come into view. 
 
A short while from Mohammed’s home, another family sits outside a small building, watching the settlers walk along the nearby hilltop. 

Children pass on their way home from school: a 2km walk on which students have also encountered threatening settlers. 

Nearby, Osama Dueis sits beside a large stack of chairs in preparation for an upcoming wedding; but even as they prepare to celebrate, Dueis fears his family will be displaced a second time. 

His first home was destroyed by the settlers in a nearby village now largely flattened and desolate, forcing him toward Jiftlik with his family and livestock just last month. 

They’ve barely had time to even make the building, a tight fit for six extended families, feel like home, but Dueis senses the weight of another looming potential displacement. 

“I mean, look at our situation, we’re left living under a plastic sheet; it’s barely a life, but we have no other choice,” he tells MEE. 

“We can’t speak out, we can’t go anywhere, we can’t even head into the mountains, nothing. Everything is so expensive - livestock feed, everything.

“There’s no such thing as privacy; nothing is private, it’s just a daily reality,” he adds about the constant monitoring and drones. 

'We can’t speak out, we can’t go anywhere, we can’t even head into the mountains, nothing'

- Osama Dueis, al-Shuneh resident

That morning, villagers captured images of the young settlers using binoculars to monitor the town, and in more recent days, the settlers attempted to steal local sheep and have thrown rocks at the Palestinians. 

They’ve now decided to keep watch together, working in rotation among the families to monitor any provocations throughout the night. 

Beyond the tense exchanges, there have also been violent altercations and the poisoning of livestock. 

The targeting of Palestinian farmers, they argue, is not only affecting people’s livelihoods but also having repercussions across the West Bank, as reports suggest settler attacks have contributed to rising livestock costs. 

“The settlers in this area…  are exceptionally aggressive, even more so than others,” Dueis said, though no arrests have been made. 

“They even targeted one of my cousins. After beating him, they asked, 'Do you know how many lives are on [my] conscience?' They take pride in this; they revel in it.”

Demolition orders and restrictions

It’s not just the new settlers placing pressure on the Palestinian residents of the Jordan Valley, whose homes are in Area C under the Oslo Accords, under Israeli security and administrative control. 

Even basic improvements to homes or infrastructure have left the community vulnerable to accusations of unauthorised construction, which is heavily restricted by Israel for Palestinians in Area C. 

Recent rains blocked local roads, but residents fear even using their tractors to clear the debris would be penalised. 

And the challenges aren’t contained to Palestinian communities. 

Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), a British NGO supporting Jiftlik, said that the mobile clinics they run among rural communities with limited access to healthcare have faced considerable delays due to checkpoints and route closures. On some days, the mobile medical clinics can’t deploy at all due to security risks. 

"What we're seeing in communities like al-Shuneh is apartheid in its most blatant form,” Aseel Baidoun, deputy director of communications at MAP, told MEE. 

'The settlers are in control': How the West Bank is being ethnically cleansed
Read More »

“Settlers can get water and electricity connected within days, while Palestinians wait years for the same basic services and live under constant threat of being driven from their land. This has a direct impact on people's health, but it also makes it harder for us to get care for those who need it.”

The harassment in Jiftlik is part of a broader surge in settler attacks that have displaced thousands of Palestinians across the West Bank since October 2023. 

The escalating violence has been met with growing international scrutiny.

Last month, the UK expanded its sanction powers over those enabling illegal Israeli outposts in the West Bank.

Then just one day before the Israeli elections, a United Nations inquiry ruled that Israel had carried out war crimes and crimes against humanity in occupied Palestinian territories, including the systematic targeting of Palestinians across the West Bank. 

Yet international condemnation and political developments have done little to change conditions on the ground.

Eisenkot, a former army chief tasked with forming a government, supports West Bank settlements, although he has criticised unauthorised outposts and what he calls “Jewish terror” against Palestinian communities. Whether the new outpost near Jiftlik can be contained remains unclear.

For Palestinians in al-Shuneh, daily life continues in the shadow of an outpost that looms over their homes and continues to expand. As Israel’s political elite jostle to form a government, little offers residents hope of relief. The settlers’ warning still hangs over the community: no political change will save them.

“Based on what we have observed in other communities, we anticipate that, moving forward, the aggression, restrictions, and acts of violence will only increase,” Dueis says.  

“There are no options; whether you head north or south, it’s all the same; everywhere you turn, there’s nowhere to go.” 

*Name has been changed to protect the identity

Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills surgeon, child and patients

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 07:53
Attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis hits intensive care and surgical wards, forcing suspension of operations
Hospital staff and others inspect the damage inside Nasser Hospital following an Israeli air strike in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on 12 November 2026 (Eyad Baba/AFP)
Off

An Israeli air strike hit Nasser Medical Complex in the Gaza Strip early on Thursday, killing at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon, a child and patients, and wounding 20 others.

The strike hit the hospital's surgical buildings at around 1 am local time. The partially functioning complex in Khan Younis remains the last major referral hospital operating in southern Gaza, despite being under extreme strain.

Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, 53, was among those killed, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. The surgeon was treating patients when the strike hit, local media reported.

At least one child and a disabled patient were also killed. Other patients and medical staff, including women and children, were wounded.

The ministry condemned the attack, describing it as a flagrant violation of international law.

“The continued targeting of hospitals and their medical facilities exacerbates the suffering of the sick and wounded, and threatens what remains of the ability of the health sector to provide its services,” it said.

Two missiles struck the building's roof, penetrating the third floor before exploding on the second, The New York Times reported.

A hospital official said the strike caused extensive damage to the intensive care and surgical wards, including both the male and female departments.

Palestinian healthcare workers are the true heroes
Read More »

The hospital's surgical ward has since been forced to suspend operations.

Hamas held the so-called Board of Peace responsible for the attack, saying it reflected Israel's continued impunity amid international silence and the failure to stop its violations.

The Israeli military confirmed the strikes, saying it had targeted “a senior terrorist and additional Hamas terrorists as they were hiding at the Nasser Hospital”. 

Ynet reported that the attack targeted Khaled Abu Anza, whom it described as the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade.

Middle East Eye could not independently verify the reports.

The Israeli military has claimed in recent months that Hamas was using Nasser Hospital for military purposes.

Similar claims have been made by the army since the start of Israel's genocide in Gaza in 2023, often preceding attacks on hospitals. The Palestinian movement has repeatedly denied them.

“The Israeli occupation's claims that Nasser Medical Complex was being used for military purposes are repeated lies intended to provide cover for the systematic targeting of the healthcare sector,” Hamas said on Thursday.

Attacks on hospitals 

The World Health Organization (WHO) says 94 percent of hospitals in Gaza have been fully or partially destroyed during Israel's genocide.

Israeli forces have also killed and abducted hundreds of doctors, nurses and other medical workers.

Nasser Hospital, the second-largest medical complex in the Gaza Strip before the war, has been targeted at least seven times since October 2023.

In August 2025, an Israeli double-tap attack on the hospital killed 20 people, including Palestinian journalists, medical staff and first responders.

Among those killed were Middle East Eye contributors Mohamed Salama and Ahmed Abu Aziz.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?
item.description:
Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?

Submitted by Paul Iddon on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 16:01
The apparent expansion of a Saudi missile facility near Riyadh has raised questions about the kingdom's military relationship with China and its rivalry with Iran
Saudi Arabia publicly displayed its Chinese-built DF-3A ballistic missiles, which boast a range of over 3,000km, during a rare military parade held on 29 April 2014 under then Crown Prince Salman bin Abdulaziz (Screengrab)
Off

Saudi Arabia is believed to be expanding its Chinese-designed ballistic missile arsenal as it faces an unprecedented barrage of missile and drone attacks from Yemen's Houthi forces.

Satellite imagery analysed by American researchers suggests the kingdom is expanding its ballistic missile plant at al-Duwadimi in Riyadh Province to build larger solid-fuel missiles capable of carrying heavier payloads across greater distances.

Fighting between the kingdom and the Iran-aligned Yemeni group has intensified since July, shattering a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. 

The Houthis have stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi cities, airports and energy infrastructure, retaliating for what they call a Saudi "blockade" of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.

Analysts have told Middle East Eye that the renewed confrontation with the Houthis has given the kingdom's arsenal added significance.

Riyadh is reported to have begun building ballistic missiles domestically with Chinese assistance in 2021, but its relationship with Beijing over the weapons dates back several decades.

In the 1980s, shortly after establishing the Royal Saudi Strategic Missile Force (RSSMF), Riyadh turned to Beijing for its first ballistic missiles. 

Beijing supplied conventional DF-3 intermediate-range ballistic missiles with an impressive range of over 2,000 miles but incredibly low accuracy.

Saudi Arabia reportedly acquired more accurate DF-21 medium-range ballistic missiles with conventional payloads in 2007.

In September, footage of missile debris in Yemen indicated that Saudi Arabia had fired a DF-15A short-range ballistic missile, potentially marking its first combat use of one of its Chinese-designed missiles.

Ameneh Mehvar, Middle East senior analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled) project, said the expansion reflected a broader Saudi strategy of diversifying its military capabilities.

"Riyadh continues to invest heavily in advanced US-supplied aircraft and defence systems, while Chinese-designed ballistic missiles provide an additional means of conducting long-range strikes without exposing aircraft to enemy air defences," Mehvar told MEE.

"Expanding domestic missile production could also give Saudi Arabia greater control over its strike capabilities and reduce its dependence on foreign deliveries," she said.

'Less exposed to geopolitical shifts'

Sim Tack, vice-president of technology and intelligence solutions at AllSource Analysis, says the satellite imagery provides a strong indication that the programme is continuing to advance.

"The expansion of infrastructure to support ballistic missile developments is notable in the sense that it confirms continued efforts to expand indigenous missile design and production capabilities," Tack told MEE.

'Domestic production capabilities and their continued development indicate most of all that Saudi Arabia intends to be self-sufficient in the production of ballistic missiles'

- Sim Tack, AllSource Analysis

"Given the regional dynamics, this intent fits with the ambitions to balance missile capabilities against Iran and its allies such as the Houthis," he said.

The expansion also points to Riyadh's ambition to source more of its missiles domestically. 

Its traditional reliance on western suppliers for military equipment has left it with limited options in the ballistic missile sector, partly because those countries have sought to avoid fuelling regional proliferation of surface-to-surface missiles and related technology.

That has helped push Saudi Arabia towards China as a discreet supplier of the weapons.

"Domestic production capabilities and their continued development indicate most of all that Saudi Arabia intends to be self-sufficient in the production of ballistic missiles," Tack said.

"Domestic production, and possibly even indigenous design, of ballistic missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to be less exposed to geopolitical shifts that could limit access to the weapon systems they would need to maintain a viable deterrent or even offensive capability," he added.

Recent developments related to US military support to Ukraine, the rapid depletion of American weapon stockpiles, and sensitivities around sourcing military equipment from China underline the increased importance of having such a localised production capability.

Deterrence and nuclear ambitions

Sebastien Roblin, a widely published military aviation journalist, argues that the purpose of the missile force should be understood in two ways: its ability to deter regional adversaries and its potential contribution to actual military operations.

"Most importantly, the missile force gives Saudi Arabia a way to practically deliver a nuclear strike, should Riyadh ever develop or otherwise acquire nuclear warheads – something looking distinctly possible today, particularly as Riyadh builds up its alliance with Pakistan," Roblin told MEE.

Egypt deployed forces to Saudi Arabia before Sisi's public pledge of military support, sources say
Read More »

"While Pakistan and Israel have independently modified US fighters for nuclear delivery, indigenously built ballistic missiles are arguably a more practical debut delivery platform, especially as Iran currently has limited ballistic missile defence capability," he said.

"Importantly, for strategic nuclear deterrence, such missiles don't have to be particularly accurate."

Solid-fuel missiles, like those Saudi Arabia is reportedly developing, offer another important advantage: they can be stored ready for launch indefinitely, unlike liquid-fuelled missiles, which require more preparation.

Keeping solid-fuel ballistic missiles on standby also reduces the likelihood that an adversary could destroy the kingdom's deterrent capability before it has a chance to launch.

"In theory, the ballistic missile force also exerts conventional deterrence," Roblin said. 

"Though in the current context of the attacks that have already rained down on cities across the Middle East in the last few years, I'm not sure Saudi conventional ballistic missiles can scare Tehran or the Houthis after what they've already endured recently."

The challenge of precision

If Riyadh intends to use its conventionally armed ballistic missiles to achieve specific military objectives, rather than simply inflict what Roblin describes as "unpredictable destruction and psychological shock", accuracy will be critical.

The DF-15A and DF-21 missiles are considerably more accurate than the older DF-3As. They can reportedly strike within 30 to 45 metres of their intended targets, less than half the length of a football field, whereas the older DF-3As could miss by several football field lengths.

But striking hardened targets, such as enemy missile silos, would require considerably greater precision to ensure a direct hit.

Yemen, Bab al-Mandab and Saudi Arabia: Tehran’s strategic calculus in the balance
Read More »

"China has achieved higher precision via satellite guidance in its later DF-15 and DF-21 series missiles, so perhaps it has or may eventually pass that technology along," Roblin said.

"Alternatively, tactical nuclear warheads can also be employed to reduce the precision needed."

Drawing on US-Israeli strikes against the Houthis and Iran since 2025, as well as four years of Russian missile attacks on Ukraine, Roblin cautions against overstating what Saudi Arabia's ballistic missile arsenal could achieve in a major conflict.

In the US-Israeli campaign against Iran, he noted, the most prominent and vulnerable targets have already been attacked. Hitting hardened underground facilities and mobile missile launchers requires persistent aerial drone surveillance and extremely rapid targeting and strike capabilities.

Concealed facilities in Iran also require sophisticated intelligence operations to identify and locate them before they can be attacked.

"Despite its comparative shortcomings, the RSSMF helps Riyadh develop a strike capability for future conflicts in which US support might be lacking; and thus might mitigate the asymmetry with Tehran's massive investment in strategic strike weapons," Roblin said.

"Remove the US from the picture, and suddenly the RSSMF might be called upon to do more heavy lifting against vulnerable static targets in future conflicts."

From deterrence to combat

Mehvar says the reported use of a Saudi DF-15A in Yemen in September, if confirmed, could signal that the kingdom's ballistic missiles are taking on a more active combat role rather than serving primarily as a deterrent.

"Overall, Riyadh appears to be broadening its military options while maintaining its longstanding reliance on US military technology and security cooperation," she said.

Tack, however, cautions that Saudi Arabia's limited history of operational ballistic missile use makes it difficult to determine how the kingdom intends to deploy the weapons.

'Riyadh appears to be broadening its military options while maintaining its longstanding reliance on US military technology and security cooperation'

- Ameneh Mehvar, Acled

"Ballistic missiles do offer methods for deep strike capabilities that Saudi Arabia has struggled to establish using their air force," he said. "Throughout Saudi operations in Yemen over the past decade, the limited effectiveness of Saudi air strikes has always stood out."

The limited accuracy and vulnerability of Saudi aircraft in contested airspace have also constrained the effectiveness of its air force. Ballistic missiles could help Riyadh overcome some of those limitations.

But doing so would require an effective intelligence capability to identify targets and guide strikes – an area in which Saudi Arabia has struggled without extensive external support.

"So while there may be an intent to apply a ballistic missile arsenal in a tactical manner on the battlefield, there are many other hurdles for Saudi Arabia to overcome to do so effectively," Tack said.

"The role of ballistic missiles as a general deterrent, and in a deep-strike role against strategic targets, appears much more viable."

A substantial missile arsenal, backed by large stockpiles, could eventually give Saudi Arabia the ability to strike Iran independently, potentially changing the balance of power between the two countries.

"Up until today, Saudi Arabia and several other countries in the region have been wholly dependent on US operations to provide a viable option to strike back at Iran," Tack said.

"Having their own viable strike options would at the very least reduce the reliance on the US in shaping negotiations with, and military action against Iran."

Sending a message

Roblin sees the reported September DF-15A launch as potentially serving two purposes: testing the weapon operationally and sending a political message to both the Houthis and Iran that Saudi Arabia has the capacity to escalate militarily.

He believes the RSSMF could carry out further combat tests to calibrate its capabilities and signal its willingness to use them.

Why have Saudi air defences failed to intercept Houthi missiles?
Read More »

"However, if Saudi Arabia is producing missiles at large enough scale - and has upgraded them to the requisite degree of accuracy for tactical effectiveness - it could choose to employ them more regularly much like the US has employed ATACMS and PrSM ballistic missiles," Roblin said.

"The capability can be a useful addition to the toolkit, though over Yemen specifically Saudi fighters arguably have enough free rein that it's not particularly urgent (despite the occasional aircraft loss)."

Saudi fighter jets can also penetrate Iranian airspace, but doing so involves greater operational risks, including evading air defences and conducting mid-air refuelling to sustain long-range missions. Ballistic missiles could offer a less complicated means of carrying out deep strikes.

Nevertheless, Roblin does not expect the missile force to replace the Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF) as the kingdom's primary striking force unless Riyadh experiences a more prolonged breakdown in relations with Washington.

"Aviation represents a more sustainable and flexible combat capability, which is why the countries you see investing more in missiles over aviation tend to be those like Iran which rightly anticipate that their manned warplanes are likely to be mostly neutralised by enemy air power," he said.

"That's not the case for the RSAF, though it certainly may benefit from working in tandem with the kingdom's surface-to-surface strike capability."

Inside Saudi Arabia

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] In the West, Jewish voices are embracing anti-Zionism. Palestinians must seize this moment
item.description:
In the West, Jewish voices are embracing anti-Zionism. Palestinians must seize this moment

Submitted by Awad Abdelfattah on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 15:53
With Israel's top global sponsor in decline, dramatic shifts in public opinion are taking place across the western world
Demonstrators wave a Palestinian flag during a nationwide day of strikes and protests in Milan, northern Italy, on 30 October 2026 (Piero Cruciatti/AFP)
Off

The publication of Benjamin Moser’s Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History comes at a significant political moment. 

Alongside the growing anti-genocide movement in the West, and the British Green Party’s recent adoption of a motion supporting a single democratic state in historic Palestine, the book helps to bring a question once marginalised in mainstream western debate into sharper focus: is Zionism an inseparable expression of Jewish identity, or a political ideology that must itself be challenged?

Moser, an American Jewish writer and Pulitzer Prize-winning biographer, approaches this question by recovering a largely suppressed tradition of Jewish opposition to Zionism. 

Through portraits of 12 Jewish figures, including Hannah Arendt, Edwin Montagu, Felicia Langer and Avi Shlaim, he demonstrates that opposition to Zionism is neither new nor alien to Jewish intellectual and political history.

The importance of his intervention goes beyond the historical recovery of individual voices. It challenges one of Zionism’s most powerful political claims: that Jewish identity, collective security and national existence necessarily require a state organised around Jewish privilege in Palestine. 

Moser’s work helps to establish that Jewish identity and opposition to Zionism are not contradictory, and that Jewish political and ethical traditions have also produced alternatives to exclusive nationalism.

This is particularly relevant after the genocide and destruction of Gaza, which have exposed the consequences of a political system founded on Palestinian dispossession, ethnic cleansing and the denial of Palestinian national rights. 

Questioning Zionism

The growing willingness of Jewish intellectuals, activists and public figures to question Zionism has contributed to a wider shift in western political discourse.

The British Greens’ decision reflects this changing atmosphere. So does the mobilisation of Americans, Palestinians, Muslims, Jewish anti-Zionists, students, trade unionists and ordinary citizens who have challenged their governments’ military and political support for Israel. 

What began, for many, as opposition to the destruction of Gaza has increasingly developed into a broader questioning of the structures of occupation, apartheid and settler-colonialism. Israel has become one of the most widely condemned countries in the world, and its founding myths are increasingly collapsing.

The central challenge is not simply to oppose Zionism, but to articulate and organise an alternative: a democratic political order in which Palestinians recover their rights

Yet an important distinction remains. Not everyone who opposes Israel’s actions supports anti-Zionism, and not everyone questioning Zionism has embraced the vision of one democratic state. 

Nevertheless, the boundaries of political debate are changing. The question is no longer confined to how Palestinians might obtain a state alongside Israel, but increasingly concerns the legitimacy of the colonial Zionist project and the political framework that governs the entire territory, from the river to the sea.

Here lies an uncomfortable paradox for the Palestinian national movement. While sections of the western left are beginning to challenge Zionism as a political framework, much of the Palestinian leadership continues to negotiate within that framework, seeking a Palestinian state alongside Israel through a partition formula that has become increasingly detached from the realities on the ground.

This is not simply an intellectual disagreement. It concerns the future of the Palestinian liberation struggle. 

International recognition of Palestinian statehood remains important and should not be dismissed. But recognition cannot be a substitute for the exercise of national rights, nor can it resolve questions about refugees, equality, dispossession and the fragmentation of the Palestinian people.

Right of return

The challenge is to move from a discussion around the “legitimacy” of partition to the legitimacy of rights. A single democratic state throughout historic Palestine - based on decolonisation, equal citizenship, collective rights and the right of return - offers a different political horizon. 

It is not a merger of two existing states, or an arrangement that preserves colonial privilege. It requires dismantling the structures that prevent Palestinians and Israeli Jews from living together as equals.

The recent Israeli elections provided another perspective on this contradiction. Despite the continuing strength of the Zionist political consensus and ever-escalating colonial brutality, Palestinian citizens of Israel participated in unprecedented numbers. 

Turnout in Arab localities reached approximately 80 percent, while Arab-led parties secured a combined 19 seats in the Knesset.

As a former head of the Balad party who advocated boycotting Israeli elections after the Knesset’s endorsement of the racist and colonial nation-state law in 2018, I regard this development as politically significant, but it must be interpreted carefully. 

It would be a mistake to read this participation as an expression of confidence in Israeli democracy or acceptance of the Zionist state. Palestinians voted in circumstances of growing existential insecurity, political repression, narrowing of the public political space, state-sponsored organised crime, and escalating attacks on their communities. 

For many, the ballot box remains one of the few available spaces through which they can defend their immediate interests, express their collective political identity, and resist the far right.

At the same time, these results expose the limitations of parliamentary politics. The increased electoral weight of Palestinian citizens has not removed the constitutional and institutional structures that deny them national equality. Nor can replacing one Israeli government with another, by itself, transform the political order.

Inseparable struggles

The deeper question is whether Palestinian participation can become part of a wider national project, rather than remaining confined to managing the consequences of colonial rule. Palestinians inside Israel cannot be reduced to a minority seeking better integration into the existing state. 

Their struggle is inseparable from that of Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank, Jerusalem, the refugee camps and the diaspora. Such an approach to the struggle and its political solution requires a radical shift in thinking, as well as an understanding that liberation is a long process that must be viewed in historical terms.

The contrast is striking. In parts of the western political arena, the legitimacy of Zionism itself is increasingly being questioned, and its lies exposed. Yet Palestinian political institutions remain largely trapped within the assumptions of the Oslo framework and the two-state paradigm.

Why Palestinian electoral gains in Israel cannot alter the racist structure of the state
Read More »

This contradiction reflects years of political fragmentation, institutional stagnation and international pressure. But it also raises an urgent question about Palestinian political responsibility: Why should western progressive movements move beyond the political assumptions of partition, while Palestinians themselves remain hesitant to reconsider them?

Moser’s book and the British Greens’ decision do not offer Palestinians a ready-made political solution. Nor should the Palestinian future depend on western political parties or Jewish intellectuals. 

Their significance lies in helping to open a political and intellectual space that Palestinians must now occupy with their own historical experience, political thinking and liberation project.

The task is to rebuild an inclusive Palestinian national movement, reconnect Palestinians across geographical and political divides, and transform the growing international solidarity movement into sustained political alliances.

Anti-Zionism without a democratic alternative and an agreed liberation vision and strategy remains incomplete. Equally, a one-state formula without decolonisation, equality and the right of return could reproduce domination under another name.

The central challenge, therefore, is not simply to oppose Zionism, but to articulate and organise an alternative: a democratic political order in which Palestinians recover their rights, and Israeli Jews - who will have to relinquish their colonial privileges - enjoy individual security, freedom and collective cultural rights, without the domination of one people over another.

The debate has begun to move beyond the legitimacy of partition. The Palestinian national movement must now confront the implications of this shift, and act in light of the dramatic changes taking place in American and European Jewish circles, as well as the evolving global solidarity movement struggling for justice and dignity. 

The remarkable results of the American elections are opening up a new horizon, as the major supporter of the genocidal regime is in rapid decline, and the continued funding of crimes against humanity in Palestine and across our region is increasingly being questioned.

item.description:
‘A slow genocide accelerated’: How Gaza’s winter ‘crisis’ is manufactured by Israel

Submitted by Katherine Hearst on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 13:41
NGOs and mutual aid groups says tens of thousands of tents lie in warehouses outside Gaza as Israeli restrictions see aid deliveries plummet in October
A displaced Palestinian child walks in a partially flooded tent camp during heavy rains in Gaza City, 7 November 2026 (Reuters/Dawoud Abu Alkas)
Off

Days ago, baby Ehab Mohammad Hamad was found by his mother, lifeless with blue lips, fingers and toes.

The six-month year old died of exposure after his family’s tent was flooded.

“No matter how hard we tried to keep the child warm and wrap him in blankets, it was all in vain,” the child’s grandmother said in a video posted by the Palestinian-led mutual aid group, the Sameer Project.

The group provided the family with a dome tent. But Hala Sabbah, who works with the organisation, said that the story fell on deaf ears.

“I was really frustrated that it wasn’t talked about,” Sabbah told MEE.

The deaths of Gaza’s babies in freezing, storm-battered tents is now becoming an annual phenomenon in the aid-starved enclave. 

For the fourth winter in a row, rains have swept through Gaza, exposing woefully inadequate supplies of materials for shelter entering the strip.

“There are tens of thousands of tents, winter coats, blankets, pallets and pallets, truckloads full of these things that are simply waiting in warehouses'

- Sean Jones, Unwra

This has forced 65 percent of the population - around 1.4m people - to shelter in makeshift shelters or tents which have been swamped in the downpour, or damaged buildings which risk collapse.

While the weather is turbocharged by a strengthening El Nino event, the paucity of aid is entirely man-made, leveraged as a pressure point by Israel over Gaza’s population.

The Israeli authorities have long restricted the entry of shelter and construction materials into Gaza, with vital equipment like tent poles and mobile homes deemed to be “dual use”.

On Sunday, the UN aid coordination office (Ocha) confirmed that 150,000 tents are prepositioned outside Gaza waiting to be delivered.

“There are tens of thousands of tents, winter coats, blankets, pallets and pallets, truckloads full of these things that are simply waiting in warehouses because they've not received normal approvals by the Israelis to let them in,” Sean Jones, director of the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (Unrwa) in Gaza told MEE.

“It's part of the trend line we see, a concerted effort just to delay,” he added.

Part of the plan

But in recent months, even fewer pallets of shelter aid appear to be struggling across the border. According to the Palestine Shelter Cluster, the number of trucks carrying shelter and household items into Gaza plummeted from 908 in December 2025, to 409 in January 2026. 

In October, weeks before the storm struck, just nine percent of aid trucks that entered that month carried shelter items.

With the Rafah crossing closed to aid in May, minimal numbers of trucks trickle through the Kerem Shalom crossing, the only route into the territory open to aid.

'This is part of Israel's plan - to push us out, to not let us bring in the aid that we need in order to respond to people'

- Shaina Low, Norwegian Refugee Council 

The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) reported in early October that the authorities were allowing just 15 trucks carrying dual-use items in one day per week. 

It warned that at the current rate of entry of dual-use items, in a best-case scenario it would take seven months for the winter aid stored in warehouses outside the strip to enter.

An assessment of shelter needs in Gaza by the Shelter Cluster in August this year revealed that an estimated 1.98 million people, 94 percent of the population, were classified in Shelter Severity Phases 3 (Crisis), 4 (Critical), or 5 (Catastrophic). 

It showed that only 10 percent of those surveyed received shelter aid in the month prior to the data collection.

While the needs in Gaza are enormous, humanitarian groups are hamstrung.

In December last year, Israel banned 37 international NGOs, including the NRC, Medecins Sans Frontieres and Oxfam, from operating in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

While the ban was subject to a temporary injunction, it is still in effect, barring the groups from bringing aid and international staff into the territory.

This and the ban issued against Unrwa - previously the main heavy lifter in terms of shelter provision in Gaza - has meant the majority of shelter aid is brought in bilaterally through committees run by the Egyptian, Qatari, Emirati and Saudi governments.

“The stockpiles inside of Gaza from INGOs are extremely low,” Shaina Low, the NRC’s communication adviser in Palestine, told MEE.

“This is part of Israel's plan to push us out, to not let us bring in the aid that we need in order to respond to people. And so the committees are the ones that seem to be able to get more aid in.”

Not fit for purpose

Due to the reduced footprint of international NGOs on the ground in Gaza, small Palestinian-led mutual aid groups like the Sameer Project have stepped into the void to buy tents on the market and distribute them. 

But scarcity has sent prices soaring. According to the Shelter Cluster, the cost of tents has rocketed by 52 percent, costing $655, while emergency shelter kits have soared by 1,233 percent to $4000.

'There had been a slow genocide throughout 2026, but over the last three to four months, we're seeing acceleration, and this is a part of their strategy'

- Hala Sabbah, Sameer Project

“A lot of tents that come in are stolen and sold on the market,” Sabbah told MEE, adding that tents are distributed to people on lists approved by the Israeli authorities.

“It’s a whole system that’s designed, you have people who are living in homes being allocated tents,” she said.

The quality of the tents has also deteriorated, as Palestinians are forced to reuse old materials.

According to the Shelter Cluster’s August assessment, over 50 percent of Palestinians sheltering in tents are using ones that are in poor or very poor condition. Fifty-four percent of them are using tents or makeshift shelters that they've been in for a year or more. 

“These are materials that only last a few months. The lifespan is really short, especially with the weather conditions in Gaza, and so people are just living in really, really difficult circumstances without access to materials to improve their living conditions,” Low said.

“We're still seeing that supplies that are entering are not necessarily fit for purpose,” she added. “Not all tents are water resistant, which means we need to divert resources like tarpaulins to reinforce them.”

According to Sabbah, many of the tents that are making it over the border appear to be made of an inferior material to previous years and are not water resistant, and require two tarpaulins to be layered over them.

Inseparable from genocide

While Palestinians in Gaza have already endured three winters in threadbare tents, this year, due to the razing of buildings and infrastructure by Israel, they are forced to camp on ever-smaller patches of land.

A spatial analysis by Forensic Architecture revealed that, over the course of the genocide, Gaza’s displaced population has increasingly been forced into low-lying areas on Gaza’s coast. 

As Israel’s expanding "yellow line" swallows up more of the territory, and the fact that much of the land is coated in debris means that they have nowhere else to go.

‘We woke up soaking wet’: Gaza’s displaced face another winter of floods and collapsed shelters
Read More »

“The tent camps now flooding are not an incidental feature of this,” Nicola Banks, Forensic Architecture's head of communications, told MEE.

“They occupy the very spaces into which Palestinians have been forcibly concentrated, often on land without the infrastructure needed to sustain life,” she said.

“The floods make visible what our investigation traces spatially, that the destruction of Gaza's built environment and the material conditions of Palestinian existence are inseparable from the ongoing genocide.”

Sabbah said that this year, the team she works with in Gaza are already exhausted, their bodies worn out by the demands of the previous three winters.

“People are taking much more sick leave than they used to in the past,” she said.  

“Their bodies are depleted. It's one thing to face winter in genocide when you're a young healthy man versus someone who has lived in these conditions for four years.

“There had been a slow genocide throughout 2026, but over the last three to four months, we're seeing acceleration, and I think this is a part of their strategy,” Sabbah told MEE.  

“They're not doing something very intense all at once because they don't want backlash from their international community.

“Its a slow genocide, accelerated.”
